(CNN) -- Massachusetts sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, challenging the constitutionality of a federal law that defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The state of Massachusetts says the Defense of Marriage Act denies same-sex couples essential rights. "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents," Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon. "Massachusetts has a single category of married persons, and we view all married persons equally and identically," she said. "DOMA divides that category into two distinct and unequal classes of marriage." The lawsuit argues that the act, which became law in 1996, denies same-sex couples essential rights and protections, including federal income tax credits, employment and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage and Social Security payments. "In enacting DOMA, Congress overstepped its authority, undermined states' efforts to recognize marriages between same-sex couples, and codified an animus towards gay and lesbian people," the state wrote in the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court. Massachusetts, the first state to legalize gay marriage, said that about 16,000 same-sex couples have been married there since 2004, when it began issuing marriage licenses. Since that time, the lawsuit said, "the security and stability of families has been strengthened in important ways throughout the state. " The state is challenging Section 3 of the law, which defines marriage as "a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife" and a spouse as "a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." Before the act, the lawsuit argues, defining marital status was the prerogative of the states. The law "eviscerated more than 200 years of federal government deference to the states with respect to defining marriage," it said. The lawsuit also argues that the law forces Massachusetts to treat same-sex married couples differently from heterosexual married couples, particularly through determining who qualifies for the state's Medicaid program, known as MassHealth, and whether a same-sex spouse of a veteran can be buried in a veteran cemetery. "But for DOMA, married individuals in same-sex relationships in the commonwealth would receive the same status, obligations, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married individuals in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal laws," the lawsuit said. The defendants named in the lawsuit include the Department of Health and Human Services, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki and the United States itself. Charles Miller, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, said the department will review the case but noted that President Obama supports the legislative repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act. In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders -- the same Boston-based group that successfully argued in 2003 for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts -- also sued the federal government over Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act. Besides Massachusetts, three other states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire will join their company when same-sex marriages become legal later this year and early next year.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Boston, targets Section 3 of the 1996 law, which defines marriage for federal purposes as the union of one man and one woman.

Congress passed the Defense of Marriage Act, commonly known as DOMA, in 1996. In addition to Section 3, the law includes a provision allowing states to decline to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere.

The Justice Department is responsible for defending federal laws in court. President Barack Obama has said he supports repealing DOMA, but his administration has maintained that the executive branch generally must defend existing statutes while they remain in effect.

## Massachusetts challenge to DOMA

On July 8, 2009, Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley filed **_Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services_** in the federal district court in Boston. It was the first lawsuit by a state challenging the federal Defense of Marriage Act.

### The state’s argument

Massachusetts had recognized same-sex marriages since 2004 following **_Goodridge v. Department of Public Health_**. But Section 3 of DOMA defined “marriage” and “spouse,” for all federal purposes, as applying only to different-sex couples.

Coakley argued that this forced Massachusetts to maintain two conflicting marital-status systems:

- Under state law, same-sex couples were legally married.
- When administering federally funded programs, Massachusetts had to treat those same couples as unmarried.

The complaint asserted that marriage and domestic relations traditionally fall within state authority and that Congress had historically accepted each state’s determination of who was married. According to Massachusetts, DOMA departed from that practice solely to deny recognition to one class of state-sanctioned marriages.

### Claimed constitutional violations

Massachusetts principally argued that Section 3:

1. **Intruded on state sovereignty under the Tenth Amendment** by overriding Massachusetts’s decisions about marriage;
2. **Violated the Spending Clause** by attaching federal funding conditions that required the state to discriminate against its own married residents; and
3. Denied equal treatment to same-sex couples whose marriages were valid under Massachusetts law.

The state identified several practical conflicts. For example, DOMA affected Massachusetts’s administration of Medicaid, taxation and employee-benefit programs, and state veterans’ cemeteries receiving federal funds. In some circumstances, the Commonwealth faced a choice between following state law and risking federal money, or complying with federal requirements and treating legally married same-sex couples as unmarried.

### District-court ruling

On July 8, 2010, U.S. District Judge Joseph Tauro ruled for Massachusetts. He concluded that Section 3 exceeded Congress’s authority under the Spending Clause and violated principles of state sovereignty protected by the Tenth Amendment.

The court held that the federal government could not use funding conditions to force Massachusetts to deny recognition to marriages the state had lawfully created. The decision was issued alongside **_Gill v. Office of Personnel Management_**, a related case brought by same-sex couples challenging DOMA on equal-protection grounds.

### Appeal

On May 31, 2012, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit unanimously affirmed that Section 3 was unconstitutional. The appellate court did not fully adopt the district court’s standalone Tenth Amendment and Spending Clause reasoning. Instead, it relied primarily on equal-protection principles, informed by DOMA’s unusual intrusion into an area traditionally regulated by the states.

By then, the Obama administration had stopped defending Section 3 after concluding that it was unconstitutional, although it continued enforcing the statute pending a final judicial decision. The Bipartisan Legal Advisory Group of the U.S. House intervened to defend it.

### Outcome and significance

The Supreme Court did not separately decide the Massachusetts case. In June 2013, it struck down Section 3 of DOMA in **_United States v. Windsor_**, holding that the federal government could not deny recognition to same-sex marriages valid under state law. The Court then declined review in the Massachusetts litigation, leaving the First Circuit’s judgment in place.

Coakley’s lawsuit was significant because it framed DOMA not only as discrimination against same-sex couples but also as a federalism problem: Congress had created a federal definition of marriage that displaced state marital determinations and compelled a state to administer programs in conflict with its own law.

**Key citations:**

- _Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health & Human Services_, 698 F. Supp. 2d 234 (D. Mass. 2010).
- _Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health & Human Services_, 682 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2012).
- _United States v. Windsor_, 570 U.S. 744 (2013).

**Massachusetts challenges federal marriage law, citing unequal treatment and state sovereignty**

**BOSTON — July 8, 2009** — Massachusetts became the first state to challenge the federal Defense of Marriage Act, arguing that the law forced the Commonwealth to discriminate against same-sex couples whose marriages were valid under state law and intruded on Massachusetts’ traditional authority to define and regulate marriage.

Attorney General Martha Coakley filed the lawsuit in federal court in Boston on behalf of the Commonwealth. The complaint targeted Section 3 of the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act, commonly known as DOMA, which defined “marriage” for all federal purposes as the union of one man and one woman and defined “spouse” as a person of the opposite sex.

“DOMA affects hundreds of rights and benefits under federal law and forces Massachusetts to engage in a kind of discrimination that is both unfair and unconstitutional,” Coakley said in announcing the case. She added: “The federal government cannot require Massachusetts to discriminate against its own citizens in order to receive federal funds.”

Massachusetts had recognized marriages between same-sex couples since May 2004, following the state Supreme Judicial Court’s decision in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health*. Under state law, those couples had the same marital status as opposite-sex couples. Under federal law, however, their marriages were treated as if they did not exist.

“Massachusetts has a single, consistent definition of marriage, and all married couples in Massachusetts should be treated equally,” Coakley said.

### Conflict between state and federal law

The lawsuit differed from private equal-protection challenges brought by individual couples. Massachusetts argued that DOMA directly interfered with state government by requiring agencies and programs to maintain two classes of legally married people.

The complaint said that when Massachusetts administered federally funded programs, it often had to choose among three unacceptable options: follow state law and risk losing federal money, follow DOMA and discriminate against same-sex spouses, or create separate administrative systems for state and federal purposes.

The state contended that this conflict violated principles of equal protection, exceeded Congress’ constitutional spending authority and infringed on powers traditionally reserved to the states under the 10th Amendment.

Gov. Deval Patrick supported the challenge, saying the federal statute prevented Massachusetts from fully honoring marriages performed under its own laws. “In Massachusetts, equal means equal,” Patrick said in connection with the case, arguing that married residents should not lose protections merely because the federal government refused to recognize their spouses.

### Benefits and protections denied

At the time, federal marital status affected more than 1,000 laws and programs. DOMA prevented same-sex married couples in Massachusetts from receiving the same federal treatment as other married couples in areas including:

- **Social Security benefits:** A surviving same-sex spouse could be denied survivor benefits, and a spouse could not claim ordinary spousal retirement benefits based on the other partner’s earnings record.

- **Health insurance and taxes:** Employer-provided health coverage for a same-sex spouse could be treated as taxable income, while comparable coverage for an opposite-sex spouse was generally excluded from federal taxable income.

- **Medicaid eligibility:** Federal rules required Massachusetts to disregard a same-sex marriage when calculating household income, assets and eligibility in certain Medicaid-related programs. That could produce different results for similarly situated married couples.

- **Veterans’ benefits and burial rights:** Federal law did not recognize a same-sex husband or wife as a veteran’s spouse. That affected access to benefits and could bar the spouse of a veteran from burial in a state veterans’ cemetery constructed or maintained with federal assistance.

- **Federal employee benefits:** Same-sex spouses could be excluded from health insurance, survivor annuities and other benefits available to the husbands and wives of federal employees.

- **Retirement and survivor protections:** Pension and retirement programs governed by federal rules could not consistently treat a same-sex spouse as a legal husband or wife.

- **Family-related federal protections:** Same-sex couples could be denied recognition in matters involving federal tax filing, immigration, family leave and other programs that used marital status to determine eligibility.

Massachusetts emphasized that the harms extended beyond individual couples. State agencies had to alter forms, computer systems, eligibility procedures and personnel policies to comply with a federal definition of marriage that contradicted state law.

One prominent example involved veterans’ cemeteries. Massachusetts maintained cemeteries supported by federal grants but wanted to allow the same-sex spouses of veterans to be buried alongside them. DOMA put the state at risk of violating federal rules or abandoning its own equal-treatment policies.

### Agencies and officials named as defendants

The lawsuit, titled *Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. United States Department of Health and Human Services*, named the United States and several federal agencies responsible for administering programs affected by DOMA. The defendants included:

- **The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**, and Secretary **Kathleen Sebelius**;
- **The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs**, and Secretary **Eric K. Shinseki**;
- **The U.S. Office of Personnel Management**, and Director **John Berry**;
- **The Social Security Administration**, and Commissioner **Michael J. Astrue**; and
- **The United States of America**.

The officials were sued in their official capacities because their departments were responsible for enforcing federal statutes and regulations that incorporated DOMA’s definition of marriage.

Massachusetts did not challenge Section 2 of DOMA, which addressed whether one state had to recognize a same-sex marriage performed in another state. Its case focused on Section 3 and the federal government’s refusal to recognize marriages that Massachusetts itself considered valid.

The Commonwealth ultimately prevailed in federal district court in 2010, when Judge Joseph L. Tauro ruled Section 3 unconstitutional in the Massachusetts case and a related case brought by married couples. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed the central ruling in 2012. In 2013, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Section 3 of DOMA in the separate case *United States v. Windsor*, clearing the way for federal recognition of lawful same-sex marriages.

# Massachusetts Challenges Federal Marriage Law Over Health Benefits and Veterans’ Burials

Massachusetts, the first state to legalize same-sex marriage, has taken its conflict with the federal Defense of Marriage Act to court, arguing that the law forces the Commonwealth to discriminate against couples it considers legally married.

In a lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston in July 2009, Massachusetts challenged Section 3 of the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act, commonly known as DOMA. That provision defined “marriage,” for purposes of federal law, as the union of one man and one woman and defined “spouse” as a person of the opposite sex.

The Commonwealth argued that the federal definition intruded on an area traditionally regulated by the states and placed Massachusetts in an untenable position: either disregard its own marriage laws or risk federal funding for programs including MassHealth and state veterans’ cemeteries.

## From *Goodridge* to the DOMA dispute

Same-sex marriage became legal in Massachusetts following the state Supreme Judicial Court’s 2003 decision in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health*. The court held that excluding same-sex couples from civil marriage violated the Massachusetts Constitution. Marriages began in May 2004.

From the state’s perspective, those couples were married in every respect. DOMA, however, required federal agencies to treat them as unmarried when administering federal statutes and programs.

That produced two competing systems. A couple could be married for state tax, inheritance and family-law purposes, yet treated as legal strangers under federal law. Because many public programs operate through federal-state partnerships, the conflict did not stop at federal benefits; it affected how Massachusetts administered its own programs.

## Effects on MassHealth

One of the state’s central examples involved MassHealth, Massachusetts’ Medicaid program. Medicaid is jointly funded by the state and federal governments and operates under federal eligibility rules.

Massachusetts generally considered a legally married couple’s relationship when determining household composition, income and eligibility for benefits. Under DOMA, however, the federal government could require the state to ignore a same-sex marriage when applying federal Medicaid standards.

The Commonwealth said this forced MassHealth to maintain different rules for different married couples. Recognizing same-sex spouses could put federal reimbursement at risk, while following the federal definition required the state to treat marriages valid under Massachusetts law as if they did not exist.

State officials argued that this was not simply an abstract disagreement over terminology. Federal Medicaid money represented a significant part of the state budget, giving Massachusetts little practical ability to reject the federal conditions.

## Veterans’ burial rights

The lawsuit also highlighted burial rights at state veterans’ cemeteries.

Massachusetts operates veterans’ cemeteries with assistance from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. State law recognizes the same-sex spouses of veterans as spouses, but federal veterans’ laws and DOMA did not extend the same recognition.

As a result, Massachusetts faced the possibility that allowing the same-sex spouse of a veteran to be buried in a state veterans’ cemetery could conflict with federal eligibility requirements or jeopardize federal support. Conversely, complying with the federal definition could require the Commonwealth to deny burial rights that it would provide to an opposite-sex spouse.

The state characterized that conflict as a direct interference with its authority to define marriage and apply its domestic-relations laws equally.

## The constitutional claims

Massachusetts relied principally on the Tenth Amendment and the Constitution’s Spending Clause.

The Commonwealth argued that marriage has historically been governed by state law and that DOMA displaced Massachusetts’ marital classifications without establishing a comprehensive federal domestic-relations system. It also contended that Congress had used federal funding to pressure the state into adopting a definition of marriage contrary to its own constitution.

In practical terms, the state said DOMA required it to choose among three unacceptable options: discriminate against married same-sex couples, violate federal program rules, or withdraw from programs supported by substantial federal funds.

The case differed from challenges brought solely by individual couples seeking federal benefits. Massachusetts asserted an injury to the state itself—its finances, its administration of public programs and its sovereign authority to determine marital status.

## Justice Department defends the law

The Justice Department moved to dismiss the case. Although President Barack Obama had said he opposed DOMA and favored its repeal, the department maintained at the time that the executive branch generally had a duty to defend federal laws while they remained in force.

Federal lawyers disputed Massachusetts’ claim that DOMA improperly commandeered state government. They argued that Congress may define terms used in federal statutes and attach conditions to federal spending programs. In their view, Massachusetts remained free to recognize same-sex marriages under state law, even if the federal government used a different definition for federal purposes.

The department also argued that participation in programs such as Medicaid was voluntary and that the funding conditions were sufficiently related to the federal programs involved. The fact that declining federal money would be financially difficult, the government maintained, did not automatically make the conditions unconstitutional.

In defending DOMA, the Justice Department emphasized Congress’ interest in maintaining a uniform federal definition of marriage and preserving the preexisting federal approach while states continued to debate same-sex marriage. At the same time, the administration stressed that its legal defense of the statute did not amount to a policy endorsement.

The Massachusetts lawsuit thus brought the conflict over DOMA beyond questions of individual federal benefits. It asked whether the federal government could use its own definition of marriage in ways that compelled a state to disregard marriages valid under state law—a dispute at the intersection of equality, federal spending and the traditional authority of states over family law.
